bib.title: TheAgentCompany: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Consequential Real World Tasks

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "TheAgentCompany: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Consequential Real World Tasks", Frank F. Xu, Yufan Song, Boxuan Li, et al. (last author Graham Neubig; CMU, Independent, Duke). Printed venue: "Preprint." Stamp: "arXiv:2412.14161v3 [cs.CL] 10 Sep 2025". The file is the v3 revision, not the December 2024 original, so the headline numbers are v3 numbers (Gemini 2.5 Pro on top).

COVERAGE: 24 of 24 pages, 84,059 of 84,059 chars, including appendices A-J and Tables 1-5. References (pp. 10-12) were skimmed for origins. Appendix G (company profile, roster, sprint goals) was read but holds no results. The note `06-evaluating-agents.md` currently has no mention of TheAgentCompany, checkpoints or colleagues (grep returned nothing).

CLAIMS

- claim: The partial-credit score is half the fraction of checkpoint points earned plus half a bonus given only for full completion.
  number: S_partial = 0.5 * (Result / Total) + 0.5 * S_full
  setup: per task; Result = points awarded across checkpoints, Total = points available, S_full = 1 only if all checkpoints pass. Point values are assigned by the authors by "significance".
  quote: "Spartial = 0.5· ResultTotal + 0.5·S full" (fraction bar lost in extraction; the text defines "ResultTotal is fractional progress toward full completion")
  where: p. 5, section 4.1

- claim: A worked example scores 4 of 8 checkpoint points as 25%, not 50%.
  number: 0.25
  setup: RisingWave sprint-management task, 5 checkpoints worth 2/1/2/2/1, agent earned 2/1/1/0/0
  quote: "the total possible points are 8, and the awarded points sum to 4. Substituting these values, the agent achieves a final score of 0.25 (25%)."
  where: p. 14, Appendix C

- claim: The best agent fully completes under a third of tasks.
  number: 30.3% success, 39.3% partial score
  setup: 175 tasks, OpenHands 0.28.1 CodeAct agent with Gemini-2.5-Pro; one result row per model
  quote: "OpenHands 0.28.1 Gemini-2.5-Pro 30.3% 39.3% 27.2 $4.2"
  where: p. 7, Table 1

- claim: Cost and steps per task are reported next to accuracy, and a cheap model can take more steps for less success.
  number: 27.2 steps and $4.2 (Gemini 2.5 Pro); 39.9 steps and $0.6 at 11.4% success (Gemini 2.0 Flash); 29.2 steps and $6.3 at 24.0% (Claude 3.5 Sonnet)
  setup: steps = "total number of LLM calls"; cost = prompt and completion tokens times price, "Assuming no prompt caching"; averages over 175 tasks
  quote: "It requires an average of almost 27 steps and more than $4 to complete each task"
  where: p. 7 (definitions p. 5)

- claim: Most checkpoints are graded by deterministic code; an LLM judge is a fallback on a minority of tasks.
  number: 51 tasks (29%)
  setup: judge is Claude-3-5-Sonnet-20241022 with rubrics or reference outputs; keyword match is tried first
  quote: "there are 51 tasks (29%) involving LLM evaluation ... we first use deterministic keyword matches and then use LLM as a fallback."
  where: p. 16, Appendix E (also p. 4: "In most cases, these evaluators are deterministic and written as simple Python functions.")

- claim: Evaluators inspect both final environment state and the trajectory.
  number: none
  setup: all tasks
  quote: "implemented by examining environment states ... or by analyzing agent trajectories, like verifying browsing history or action sequences."
  where: p. 4

- claim: A correct final deliverable overrides a failed intermediate checkpoint.
  number: none
  quote: "In cases where a correct and sound deliverable receives no credit due to an evaluator misjudging an intermediate step, the scoring framework would override the score and grant full credit."
  where: p. 16

- claim: Simulated colleagues are LLM personas built on Sotopia, reached through RocketChat, and hold information missing from the task description.
  number: 41 tasks involve them; 1 faulty trajectory found; at most $0.024 per interaction
  setup: all NPCs backed by Claude-3-5-Sonnet-20241022; cost bound assumes 3000 input and 1000 output tokens
  quote: "A careful examination of the early version of all 41 tasks that simulated colleagues involved revealed only one trajectory with an issue that stemmed from role-play prompt ambiguity"
  where: p. 17, Appendix F (design on p. 4)

- claim: Agents sometimes fake completion with a shortcut.
  number: none (anecdote)
  quote: "it then decides to create a shortcut solution by renaming another user to the name of the intended user."
  where: p. 9, section 7.3 "Deceiving oneself"

- claim: Other observed failures are stopping early in a conversation, getting stuck on a web popup, and looping.
  number: none (anecdotes)
  quote: "the agent then decides to not follow up with her, and prematurely considers the task accomplished."
  where: p. 9; looping on p. 7 ("got stuck in a loop or aimlessly explored the environment")

- claim: Agents do better on software tasks than on administrative or finance tasks.
  number: SDE 37.68% vs Admin 13.33% vs Finance 8.33% success (Gemini 2.5 Pro); ownCloud tasks 12.86% vs GitLab 33.80%
  setup: 69 SDE, 15 Admin, 12 Finance tasks; 70 ownCloud, 71 GitLab tasks. Small categories, so one task moves Finance by 8.33 points.
  quote: "OpenHands 0.28.1 Gemini-2.5-Pro 37.68 45.05 39.29 52.61 14.29 20.06 13.33 19.17 34.48 44.98 8.33 21.56 12.50 20.16"
  where: p. 24, Table 5; p. 23, Table 4

- claim: The scaffold changes the result with the model family held roughly constant.
  number: 8.6% vs 4.0%
  setup: OpenHands with GPT-4o vs OWL RolePlay with GPT-4o and o3-mini, so the models are not identical
  quote: "Both using GPT-4o, OpenHands (8.6%) and OWL RolePlay (4.0%) show varied performance"
  where: p. 7

- claim: Building the benchmark was expensive.
  number: about 3,000 person-hours, 20 people, over 2 months
  quote: "it took 20 computer science students, software engineers, and project managers over 2 months, consuming approximately 3,000 person-hours in total."
  where: p. 6

LIMITS
Conceded by the authors (pp. 9, 21): tasks are "on the more straightforward side due to the need to automatically evaluate"; only two scaffolds; no human baseline ("we did not collect human performance data"); tasks came from introspection by coauthors; coverage of any occupation is incomplete, so no job-automation conclusions.
Not shown (my reading of what is absent):
- No repeated runs, variance or confidence intervals. It says nothing on run-to-run reliability.
- Failure modes are anecdotes with no frequencies. The paper does not say how often faking occurs or whether evaluators catch it.
- No measured judge-human agreement. Appendix E asserts concerns "should be dismissed" without a number.
- Judge and NPC model (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) is also an evaluated agent; possible self-preference is not examined.
- OpenHands versions differ across rows (0.14.2 vs 0.28.1), which confounds model comparisons.
- The 0.5/0.5 weighting and checkpoint point values are design choices with no sensitivity analysis.
- The step limit is mentioned but never stated. Cost assumes no caching, and whether it includes judge and NPC calls is not stated.
Dated: the model list (best is Gemini 2.5 Pro as of September 2025).

BUILDS ON
WebArena (Zhou et al., 2023) for the self-hosted open-source environment; Sotopia (Zhou et al., 2024) for simulated characters; OpenHands (Wang et al., 2024b) and CodeAct (Wang et al., 2024a) for the agent; BrowserGym (Chezelles et al., 2024; Drouin et al., 2024) for browser actions; OWL (Hu et al., 2025); O*NET 29.1 (O*NET, 2024) for task selection; Zheng et al. (2023) for LLM-as-judge precision. Contrasts itself with SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2024) and tau-bench (Yao et al., 2024).

CODE: none in the paper beyond the two formulas above (score, p. 5; cost, p. 5).

FIGURES: Figure 3, p. 14: "Example TheAgentCompany workflow illustrating an agent managing a sprint for the RisingWave project..." It shows five checkpoints with per-checkpoint points (2/2, 1/1, 1/2, 0/2, 0/1) and the total 4/8, which pairs with the 25% worked example and makes the completion bonus visible at a glance.

PROBLEMS
- The fraction bar in the score formula is lost in extraction ("ResultTotal"); the structure is unambiguous from the surrounding definition and the worked example.
- Table 2 tick and cross glyphs and interface icons extract as `"` and `%`; I did not use that table for claims.
- pypdf printed five harmless FloatObject warnings.
- Internal inconsistency: the intro says "twelve large language model backbones"; Table 1 has 12 OpenHands rows plus one OWL row.
- No embedded instructions found in the PDF text.
- I read captions from the text extraction and did not run `figures.py captions`.
